notes.subject: plate
notes.text: Long white plates with a blue strip; yellow commercial plates; and 'parrot' plates with a yellow section on the left, unique here.

notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: White bollard with a yellow reflector and a dark orange stripe, unique to this country; a green variant also exists.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Low direction signs framed by pipes, red and white or blue and white, with an arrow built into the background and often a road number.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: A signpost where the pipe frame bends around the sign is unique here.

notes.subject: line
notes.text: Outer road lines often consist of small white squares, a strong identifier.

notes.subject: line
notes.text: All lines are white and double middle lines are very common.

notes.subject: guardrail
notes.text: Plain square B-type guardrails with no reflectors, used by very few European countries.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Pedestrian signs have 5 stripes, the first and fifth touching the triangle's edge; neighbours to the north have 4.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: A distinctive town entry sign is crossed by a red slash on leaving.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Bus stops have black and yellow signs with a schedule below; an older blue and white version exists.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Red and white chevrons, often low to the ground.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Street names often end in vej and street signs are usually blue with white text.

notes.subject: language
notes.text: A North Germanic language using Æ, Ø and Å, but not Ä or Ö.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Gas brands Ingo, OK, Uno-X and Yx appear, each shared with one other country.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: The national postal company uses unique mailboxes.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Ordinary street-level utility poles are rare; big towering overhead lines run through the countryside, often near highways.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Bicycle paths often run beside the road.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Red brick buildings with orange, dark brown or black roof tiles; thatched roofs and timber frames are also seen.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Grey corrugated roofs sometimes appear, similar to those in the Baltic states.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Generally flat with wide open fields between towns and open suburbs.

notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: Rare stone bollards, sometimes with red tops, stand near bike paths.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Roads are numbered east to west; those starting 2 to 5 group by region, and the island in the east only has roads starting with 1.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Highways labelled O1 to O4 ring bigger cities, numbers rising from the centre.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Six regions each have their own bus company, colour scheme and bus stop sign.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Bus stops on the Baltic island have a green, red and white scheme, and green bicycle signs appear.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Traditional seaweed roofs made of eelgrass are found on the island of Læsø.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: The island of Anholt has only generation 2 coverage, gloomy and overcast, with sandy roadsides.
